title: Hayley:
headline: In South Africa, denial ended only when the people who did harm confirmed what survivors said.
story: Hayley is a South African human-rights lawyer. Her lesson from the Truth Commission: South Africa had to read the page of history before turning it. Survivors told the truth, and many still denied it, until the perpetrators confirmed it.
Truth-telling matters, but it is not enough. Reconciliation is a process, not an event, and it lasts when it comes from the bottom up. Serious, clear, and still hopeful.

Auto-transcript of FX6_LVH_6402.MXF (Hayley, Brussels, 15 Sep 2026). Times are mm:ss in the source file. Every line is labelled "Interviewee" in the source. Interviewer and chatter: 02:48-03:23 (question + noise check), 05:05-05:19 (question), 06:34-07:17 (retake chatter + question).
[00:11] So in South Africa I am a human rights lawyer and a mediation attorney and the work that
[00:18] I do is essentially to focus on public interest test case litigation within the transitional
[00:26] justice context, which effectively means litigating cases in South Africa's constitutional court that
[00:32] will make law or change law to advance the substantive equality of human beings in our
[00:39] country and also to be involved in civil society activism, advocacy and law reform. In terms of one
[00:49] of the most valuable lessons that I've learned, I think there are two. The one is that discrimination
[00:56] is intersectional and as are the harms of intersectional discrimination, intersectional
[01:03] and compounding and in fact multiplicative themselves and that in order to create mechanisms
[01:13] and transformative remedies that can enhance substantive equality, alleviate the burdens
[01:20] and the wounds and the traumas of people's lives and hopefully transform them or assist in
[01:28] transforming them for the better when one needs to take account of the intersectionality of harms
[01:35] and the intersectionality of trauma. And the second lesson would be that justice means very
[01:42] different things to different people and that there are very many different forms of justice.
[01:47] So for some people it might be criminal justice, for others civil justice with damages awards,
[01:53] for others it may be having unanswered questions answered and truth told, for others it might be
[02:03] people who have harmed them, not just telling the truth but taking accountability. For other people
[02:11] it might be an apology, one that is genuine, for somebody else it might be reparations whether
[02:20] done by perpetrators or whether at a state level and for others still it might be transformative
[02:27] justice, something that looks to the future and says how can we transform the lives of oneself
[02:36] or one's children or other family members so that their chances in the future are enhanced and their
[02:44] chances of living a life hopefully with less trauma and less pain and more opportunities
[02:48] are significantly enhanced. (Interviewer:) Could you tell us a little bit about the work of the commission,
[02:57] what it wanted to do and here I'm thinking what you were saying about creating shared memory and
[03:02] about the no space for denial but whatever else you want to say and its effects, what it managed
[03:08] to do. So the South African Truth Commission. There's a noise, are you hearing? But it was like
[03:17] this before right? And it's off. Yeah it's very low frequency. The South African Truth Commission
[03:27] was tasked with advancing and promoting peace, national unity and reconciliation in South Africa
[03:37] at the end of apartheid and important about that was that it was not tasked with achieving it,
[03:44] it was tasked with promoting and advancing it in a society that was deeply divided and deeply
[03:49] wounded and with that came the task of creating a shared and complex memory or narrative of what
[04:01] had happened. While it was recognised that South Africa needed to turn the page of history,
[04:10] it was acknowledged that first that page needed to be read and what that meant effectively was
[04:16] the need to challenge denial around the gross human rights violations that had been committed
[04:22] throughout apartheid, not only by the state security forces but by the liberation movements
[04:28] in the course of the just war as well. What was really interesting in the South African commission
[04:35] was that as victims or survivors testified about what had happened to them or their family members,
[04:43] there was still an immense amount of denial particularly amongst white South Africans and
[04:47] and some people said that survivors were either lying or exaggerating the extent of the gross
[04:52] human rights abuses and it was only when the perpetrators began testifying in their amnesty
[04:58] hearings and confirmed what victims or survivors had been saying that denial became absolutely
[05:05] impossible. (Interviewer:) What is a peace-building approach that you've seen work in South Africa that you
[05:14] believe could make a difference? I think there are a number. I think truth commissions are
[05:22] meaningful but I think that they are not enough. I think they're meaningful in terms of giving
[05:27] people a space to tell what is on their hearts and what they've been carrying for many years
[05:33] and to do so publicly and for that to be cathartic. I think it's important in terms of truth,
[05:38] not just truth telling but also truth seeking, but it's not enough and I think it needs to be
[05:44] coupled with a genuine reparations program, with institutional reform, with justice of many other
[05:50] kinds. I also think that civil society remains incredibly important in terms of peace-building
[06:00] and nation-building and an acknowledgement that reconciliation is not an event,
[06:07] that reconciliation is a process and a long-term process that comes about through consistent and
[06:13] trustworthy behavior over time that acknowledges what has happened in the past and really does
[06:23] make an effort on behalf of, you know, not just at the national level but interpersonal.
[06:34]-[07:13] (retake chatter and the next question: not used)
[07:13] you would urge policymakers to take right now? I think a tangible policy action that I would urge
[07:23] policymakers to take is to continue engaging with civil society or if they are not engaging
[07:29] sufficiently with a broad range of civil society to do so. I think it's more likely that any measures
[07:36] agreed upon will be sustainable if they are not just imposed from the top down but actually come
[07:43] from the bottom up as well and I think that it's only through hearing the, you know,
[07:49] those that are working close to the ground that one truly knows what's going on in society
[07:54] and what people's needs really are.
